source_text: Nunc ad diuina testimonia transeamus. sed prius unum proferam, quod est simile diuino et ob nimiam uetustatem et quod is quem nominabo ex hominibus in deos relatus est.. apud Ciceronem U. Cotta pontifex disputans contra Stoicos de religionibus et uarietate opinionum quae solent esse de diis, ut more Academicorum omnia faceret incerta, quinque fuisse Mercurios ait et enumeratis per ordinem quattuor quintum fuisse eum a quo sit Argus occisus; ob eamque causam in Aegyptum profugisse atque Aegyptiis leges ac litteras tradidisse. hunc Aegyptii Thoyth appellant, a quo apud eos primus anni sui mensis id est September nomen accepit. idem oppidum condidit, quod etiam nunc graece uocatur Mercurii ciuitas, et Pheneatae colunt eum religiose. qui tametsi homo fuit, antiquissimus tamen et instructissimus omni genere doctrinae adeo, ut ei multarum rerum et artium scientia Trismegisto cognomen inponeret. hic scripsit libros et quidem multos ad cognitionem diuinarum rerum pertinentes, in quibus maiestatem summi ac singularis dei asserit isdemque nominibus appellat quibus nos dominum et patrem. ac ne quis nomen eius requireret, άνώνυμον esse dixit, eo quod nominis proprietate non egeat, ob ipsam scilicet unitatem. ipsius haec uerba sunt: o se Oso; είς, b δὲ είς όνόματος ou προσδέεται έστι ykp o wv ὰνώνυμος. deo igitur nomen (non) est, quia solus est, nec opus est proprio uocabulo, nisi cum discrimen exigit multitudo, ut unam quamque personam sua nota et appellatione designes. deo autem, quia semper unus est, proprium nomen est deus. Superest de responsis sacrisque carminibus testimonia quae sunt multo certiora proferre. nam fortasse ii contra quos agimus nec poetis putent esse credendum tamquam uana fingentibus nec philosophis, quod errare potuerint, quia et ipsi homines fuerint. M. Varro, quo nemo umquam doctior ne apud Graecos quidem uixit, in libris rerum diuinarum quos ad C. Caesarem pontificem maximum scripsit, cum de quindecimuiris loqueretur, Sibyllinos libros ait non fuisse unius Sibyllae, sed appellari uno nomine Sibyllinos, quod omnes feminae uates Sibyllae sint a ueteribus nuncupatae uel ab unius Delphidis nomine uel a consiliis deorum enuntiandis. atouq enim deos, non Osouc, et consilium non βουλήν, sed βούλλαν appellabant Aeolico genere sermonis. itaque Sibyllam dictam esse quasi θεοβούλην. ceterum Sibyllas decem numero fuisse, easque omnes enumerauit sub auctoribus qui de singulis scriptitauerint. primam fuisse de Persis, cuius mentionem fecerit Nicanor, qui res gestas Alexandri Macedonis scripsit; secundam Libyssam, cuius meminerit Euripides in Lamiae prologo; tertiam Delphida, de qua Chrysippus loquatur in eo libro quem de diuinatione conposuit; quartam Cimmeriam in Italia, quam Naeuius in libris belli Punici, Piso in annalibus nominet; quintam Erythraeam, quam Apollodorus Erythraeus adfirmet suam fuisse ciuem eamque Grais Ilium petentibus uaticinatam et perituram esse Troiam et Homerum mendacia scripturum; sextam Samiam, de qua scribat Eratosthenes in antiquis annalibus Samiorum repperisse so scriptum; septimam Cumanam nomine Amaltheam, quae ab aliis Herophile uel Demophile nominetur, eamque nouem libros attulisse ad regem Tarquinium Priscum ac pro iis trecentos philippeos postulasse regemque aspernatum pretii magnitudinem derisisse mulieris insaniam; illam in conspectu regis tris combussisse ac pro reliquis idem pretium poposcisse; Tarquinium multo magis insanire mulierem putauisse; quae denuo tribus aliis exustis cum in eodem pretio perseueraret, motum esse regem ac residuos trecentis aureis emisse; quorum postea numerus sit auctus, Capitolio refecto, quod ex omnibus ciuitatibus et Italicis et Graecis praecipueque Erythraeis coacti adlatique sunt Romam cuiuscumque Sibyllae nomine fuerunt; octauam Hellespontiam in agro Troiano natam, uico Marmesso circa oppidum Gergithium, quam scribat Heraclides Ponticus Solonis et Cyri fuisse temporibus; nonam Phrygiam, quae uaticinata sit Ancyrae; decimam Tiburtem nomine Albuneam, quae Tiburi colatur ut dea iuxta ripas amnis Anienis, cuius in gurgite simulacrum eius inuentum esse dicitur tenens in manu librum. arum onmium Sibyllarum carmina et teruntur et habentur, praeterquam Cymaeae, cuius libri a Romanis occultantur nec eos ab ullo nisi a quindecimuiris inspici fas habent. et sunt singularum singuli libri: quos, quia Sibyllae nomine inscribuntur, unius esse credunt, suntque confusi nec discerni ac suum cuique adsignari potest nisi Erythraeae, quae et nomen suum uerum carmini inseruit et Erythraeam se nominatuiri praelocuta est, cum esset orta Babylone. sed et IlOS confuse Sibyllam dicemus, sicubi testimoniis earum ruent abutendum. omnes igitur hae Sibyllae unum deum praedicant, maxime tamen Erythraea, quae celebrior inter ceteras ac nobilior habetur, siquidem Fenestella diligentissimus scriptor de quindecim uiris dicens ait restituto Capitolio rettulisse ad senatum C. Curionem consulem, ut legati Erythras mitterentur, qui carmina Sibyllae conquisita Romam deportarent: itaque missos esse P. Gabinium M. Otacilium L. Valerium, qui descriptos a priuatis uersus circa mille Romam deportarunt. idem dixisse Varronem supra ostendimus. in his ergo uersibus quos Romam legati adtulerunt de uno deo haec sunt testimonia: εἷς θεός, ὂς μόνος ἄρχει, ὐπερμεγέθης ἀγένητος. hunc esse solum summum deum, qui caelum fecerit luminibusque distinxerit: ἀλλὰ θεὸς μόνος εἶς πανυπέρτατος, ὃς πεποίηκεν οὐρανὸν ἡέλιὸν τε καὶ ἀστέρας, ἠδέ σελήνην, καρποφόρον γαῖαν τε καὶ ὕδατος οἴδματα πόντου. qui quoniam solus sit aedificator mundi et artifex rerum uel quibus constat uel quae in eo sunt, solum coli oportere testatur: αὐτὸν τὸν μόνον ὄντα σέβεσθ᾽ ἡγήτορα κόσμου. ὃς μόνος εἰς αἰῶνα καὶ ἐξ αἰῶνος ἐτύχθη. item alia Sibylla quaecumque est cum perferre se ad homines uocem dei diceret, sic ait: μοῦνος γὰρ θεὸς εἰμὶ καὶ οὐκ ἔστι θεὸς ἄλλος. Exequerer nunc testimonia ceterarum, nisi et haec sufticerent et illa opportunioribus locis reseruarem. sed cum defendamus causam ueritatis aput eos qui aberrantes a ueritate falsis religionibus seruiunt, quod genus probationis aduersus eos magis adhibere debemus quam ut eos deorum suorum testimoniis reuincamus?
pass_a_gloss: Now let us proceed to divine testimonies. But first, I will bring forth one thing which is similar to the divine and, because of its great antiquity, and because the one whom I will name was transferred from men to gods. In Cicero, U. Cotta, a pontiff, arguing against the Stoics about religions and the variety of opinions which are accustomed to be about the gods, so that, in the manner of the Academics, he might make all things uncertain, says that there were five Mercurys and, having enumerated four in order, the fifth was the one by whom Argus was killed; and because of this cause, he fled to Egypt and handed over laws and letters to the Egyptians. The Egyptians call this one Thoyth, from whom the first month of their year, that is, September, received its name. The same one founded a city, which is even now called the city of Mercury in Greek, and the Pheneatae worship him religiously. Who, although he was a man, was nevertheless most ancient and most instructed in every kind of doctrine, so that he was given the surname Trismegistus because of his knowledge of many things and arts. This one wrote books, and indeed many, pertaining to the knowledge of divine things, in which he asserts the majesty of the highest and singular God and calls him by the same names by which we call the Lord and Father. And lest anyone might seek his name, he said that it is anonymous, because it does not need the property of a name, on account of its unity. His words are these: 'O the one God; one, indeed, is the one who does not need a name.' Therefore, God does not have a name, because he is alone, nor is a proper word needed, except when a multitude demands a distinction, so that you might designate each person with their own mark and appellation. But for God, because he is always one, the proper name is God. It remains to bring forth testimonies which are much more certain from the sacred and prophetic poems. For perhaps those against whom we are arguing do not think that poets should be believed, as if they were inventing vain things, nor philosophers, because they could have erred, since they also were men. M. Varro, than whom no one was ever more learned, not even among the Greeks, in the books of divine things which he wrote to C. Caesar, the pontifex maximus, when he was speaking about the quindecimvirs, says that the Sibylline books were not of one Sibyl, but are called by one name Sibylline, because all the female prophets are called Sibyls by the ancients, either from the name of one Delphid or from the counsels of the gods being announced. For they called the gods not Osouc, but theos, and counsel not boulēn, but boulēn, in the Aeolic kind of speech. And so, the Sibyl is said to be, as it were, theoboulē. Moreover, there were ten Sibyls in number, and he enumerated all of them under the authors who wrote about each one. The first was from Persia, whom Nicanor mentioned, who wrote about the deeds of Alexander of Macedon; the second was Libyssa, whom Euripides remembered in the prologue of Lamia; the third was Delphid, about whom Chrysippus spoke in that book which he composed about divination; the fourth was Cimmerian in Italy, whom Naevius named in the books of the Punic war, and Piso in the annals; the fifth was Erythraean, whom Apollodorus of Erythrae affirmed was his fellow citizen, and who prophesied to the Greeks who were going to Ilium that Troy would be destroyed and that Homer would write falsehoods; the sixth was Samian, about whom Eratosthenes wrote in the ancient annals of the Samians; the seventh was Cumana, named Amalthea, who was also named Herophile or Demophile by others, and who brought nine books to king Tarquinius Priscus and demanded three hundred philippeos for them, and the king, despising the magnitude of the price, ridiculed the woman's insanity; she, having burned three of them in the sight of the king, asked the same price for the remaining ones; Tarquinius thought the woman was even more insane; who, when she persevered in the same price after burning three more, moved the king, and the remaining ones were bought for three hundred gold pieces; the number of which was later increased, the Capitol being rebuilt, which was brought and collected from all the cities, both Italian and Greek, and especially Erythraean, to Rome, under the name of whatever Sibyl they were; the eighth was Hellespontian, born in the Trojan field, in the village Marmesso, near the city Gergithium, whom Heraclides of Pontus wrote was in the time of Solon and Cyrus; the ninth was Phrygian, who prophesied in Ancyra; the tenth was Tiburtine, named Albunea, who is worshiped as a goddess in Tibur, near the banks of the river Anio, whose image is said to have been found in the whirlpool, holding a book in her hand. And the poems of all the Sibyls are both worn out and possessed, except for those of the Cumana, whose books are hidden by the Romans, and it is not lawful for anyone to inspect them except the quindecimvirs. And there are individual books of each one: which, because they are inscribed with the name of the Sibyls, are believed to be of one, and are confused, nor can they be discerned and assigned to each one, except for the Erythraean, who inserted her true name into the poem and proclaimed that she was named Erythraea, when she was born in Babylon. But also, we will confusedly call the Sibyl, wherever we will use their testimonies. Therefore, all these Sibyls proclaim one God, especially the Erythraean, who is considered more famous and noble among the others, since Fenestella, a most diligent writer, saying that the quindecimvirs restored the Capitol, reported to the senate that the consul C. Curio sent legates to Erythrae, who brought the poems of the Sibyl to Rome: and so, P. Gabinius, M. Otacilius, and L. Valerius were sent, who brought about a thousand verses, written by private individuals, to Rome. The same Varro said above. In these verses, which the legates brought to Rome, there are these testimonies about one God: 'One God, who alone rules, immense, unbegotten.' That this one is the only highest God, who made the heaven and distinguished it with lights: 'But God alone is one, most high, who made the heaven, the sun, and the stars, and the moon, and the fruitful earth, and the waters of the sea.' Who, since he is alone the builder of the world and the artisan of things, either which consist in it or which are in it, testifies that he alone should be worshiped: 'Honor the one who is the only ruler of the world.' Who alone is from eternity and to eternity. Also, another Sibyl, whoever she is, when she said that she was bringing the voice of God to men, says thus: 'For I am the only God, and there is no other God.' I would now bring forth the testimonies of the other Sibyls, if these were not sufficient and if I were reserving those for more opportune places. But since we are defending the cause of truth against those who, straying from the truth, serve false religions, what kind of proof ought we to use more against them than to convict them with the testimonies of their own gods?
pass_b_english: Now we turn to the divine testimonies, but first I must produce one witness who resembles them both in his great antiquity and in the fact that he was elevated from humanity to divinity. In Cicero's work, the pontiff U. Cotta argues against the Stoics on the subject of religion and the variety of opinions about the gods; adopting the Academic method of making everything uncertain, he declares that there were five Mercurys. After listing four in order, he identifies the fifth as the one who killed Argus, fled to Egypt, and gave the Egyptians their laws and letters. The Egyptians call him Thoyth, and from him their first month—September—took its name. He also founded a city still called in Greek the City of Mercury, and the Pheneatae worship him devoutly. Though he was a man, he was the most ancient and thoroughly versed in every kind of learning, so that his knowledge of many arts and sciences earned him the surname Trismegistus. He wrote many books on the knowledge of divine things, in which he asserts the majesty of the highest and singular God, calling him by the very names we use for the Lord and Father. Lest anyone ask for his name, he said it is anonymous, because it does not require the property of a name, owing to its very unity. His words are: "O the one God; one, indeed, is the one who does not need a name." Therefore God has no name, because he is alone, nor is a proper title needed, except when a multitude demands a distinction so that each person may be designated by a unique mark and appellation. But for God, because he is always one, the proper name is God.

It remains to bring forward testimonies from the sacred and prophetic poems, which are far more certain. Perhaps those against whom we argue do not think poets should be trusted, as if they invent vain things, nor philosophers, since they could have erred, being men themselves. Marcus Varro, than whom no one more learned ever lived—not even among the Greeks—in his books on divine matters addressed to Gaius Caesar the pontifex maximus, when speaking of the quindecimvirs, says the Sibylline books were not the work of one Sibyl, but are called by the single name "Sibylline" because all female prophets were called Sibyls by the ancients, either from the name of one Delphid or from the announcing of the counsels of the gods. For they called the gods not Osouc but theos, and counsel not boulēn but boulēn, in the Aeolic dialect. Thus the Sibyl is said to be, as it were, theoboulē. Moreover, there were ten Sibyls in number, and he enumerated them all under the authors who wrote about each. The first was from Persia, mentioned by Nicanor, who wrote the deeds of Alexander of Macedon; the second was Libyssa, whom Euripides recalls in the prologue of the Lamia; the third was Delphid, of whom Chrysippus speaks in his book on divination; the fourth was the Cimmerian in Italy, named by Naevius in his books on the Punic War and by Piso in his annals; the fifth was the Erythraean, whom Apollodorus of Erythrae affirms was his fellow citizen, and who prophesied to the Greeks sailing for Ilium that Troy would fall and that Homer would write falsehoods; the sixth was the Samian, of whom Eratosthenes writes in the ancient annals of the Samians; the seventh was the Cumaean, named Amalthea, also called Herophile or Demophile by others, who brought nine books to King Tarquinius Priscus and demanded three hundred philippeos for them. The king despised the magnitude of the price and ridiculed the woman's insanity; she burned three of them in his sight and asked the same price for the remaining six. Tarquinius thought her even more insane; but when she persevered at the same price after burning three more, he was moved and bought the surviving books for three hundred gold pieces. Their number was later increased when the Capitol was rebuilt, for they were collected and brought to Rome from all cities, Italian and Greek, and especially from Erythrae, under the name of whatever Sibyl they were. The eighth was the Hellespontian, born in the Troad, in the village of Marmesso near the city of Gergithium, whom Heraclides of Pontus places in the time of Solon and Cyrus; the ninth was the Phrygian, who prophesied at Ancyra; the tenth was the Tiburtine, named Albunea, worshiped as a goddess at Tibur near the banks of the Anio, whose image is said to have been found in the whirlpool holding a book in her hand. The poems of all the Sibyls are both worn and preserved, except those of the Cumaean, whose books the Romans keep hidden, and it is not lawful for anyone but the quindecimvirs to inspect them. There are individual books for each Sibyl, but because they are all inscribed with the name of the Sibyls, they are believed to be the work of one, and are confused, nor can they be distinguished and assigned to each—except for the Erythraean, who inserted her true name into the poem and proclaimed herself the Erythraean, though she was born in Babylon. Even so, we will speak of the Sibyl indistinctly whenever we must use their testimonies.

All these Sibyls proclaim one God, especially the Erythraean, who is the most famous and noble among them. The diligent writer Fenestella, in his account of the quindecimvirs, says that when the Capitol was restored, the consul Gaius Curio reported to the senate that legates should be sent to Erythrae to recover the Sibyl's poems and bring them to Rome. Accordingly Publius Gabinius, Marcus Otacilius, and Lucius Valerius were dispatched; they brought back about a thousand verses copied from private collections. Varro confirms this above. In these verses which the legates brought to Rome, the testimonies concerning one God are these: "One God, who alone rules, immense, unbegotten." This is the only highest God, who made heaven and distinguished it with lights: "But God alone is one, most high, who made heaven, the sun, and the stars, the moon, the fruitful earth, and the waters of the sea." Since he alone is the builder of the world and the artisan of all things, whether those that constitute it or those within it, he testifies that he alone must be worshiped: "Honor the one who is the only ruler of the world." He alone is from eternity and to eternity. Likewise another Sibyl, whoever she may be, when she declared that she was bringing the voice of God to men, said: "For I am the only God, and there is no other God." I would now produce the testimonies of the other Sibyls, were these not sufficient and were I not reserving those for more opportune places. But since we defend the cause of truth against those who, straying from the truth, serve false religions, what kind of proof ought we to employ against them more than to convict them by the testimonies of their own gods?
